title: Good Leaders Develop an Editorial Mindset
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article positions editing, not producing, as the most important skill in a leader's toolkit. Leaders with an editorial mindset decide what matters, sharpen how ideas are communicated, and cut away anything that doesn't serve the team's goals, applying this discipline to decisions, proposals, meetings, and messages alike. The author notes that editing and writing are different skill sets, so a leader doesn't need to be a great producer of ideas to be a great editor of other people's work. The piece closes by urging readers to consciously adopt this editorial identity as a daily practice.
points: The most important leadership skill may be editing, not producing, ideas and content
Editor-leaders decide what matters, sharpen communication, and cut what doesn't serve the goal
Editorially skilled leaders run tighter meetings by curating what deserves discussion time
Editing and writing are different skills; leaders don't need to be great producers to be great editors
quotes: To uphold their commitment to quality, good leaders operate as editors. It may be the most important slice of what they do as leaders.
As editors, leaders shape and refine the messages, ideas, and viewpoints of others to make them stronger and more impactful.
Not surprisingly, editorially skilled leaders run better meetings. They curate the most important topics and content and cut away any unnecessary issues or discussion points
You don’t have to be a great writer to be a great editor. That’s because they involve different skill sets.
If the essence of great work is continual revising and improvement, exceptional leaders do the editing.
